newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives attack Labour spending plans.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives attack Labour spending plans.

text.p: Britain's Conservative party tried on Tuesday to regain the initiative on the crucial electoral battleground of tax-and-spending policy by exposing what it said was a big black hole in the Labour opposition's budget plans.

Gordon Brown, Labour's economic spokesman, put the ruling party on the back foot last month by promising a Labour government would not only freeze income tax rates but would also stick to Conservative spending plans for the next two years.
But Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke mounted a counter-offensive by detailing what he said was a 12 billion pound ($20 billion) black hole in Brown's spending plans.
"It is proof positive that Mr Brown's sums just don't add up," Clarke told a news conference. "If Gordon Brown were an accountant he'd be sued for professional malpractice."
By attacking Labour on tax and spending, the finance minister was hoping to capitalise on poll evidence that many voters still distrust the main opposition party on tax.
An NOP poll for Reuters released on Tuesday put Labour's support at 50 percent, against 30 percent for the Conservatives.
But 32 percent of those questioned felt total taxes would be higher under a Labour government compared with 19 percent who felt they would pay more under the Conservatives.

Clarke accused Brown of making serious errors that would leave a 12.37 billion pound gap in Labour's public finances over the next two years if it won the election, which is likely to be held on May 1.
Clarke identified four types of "black hole" in Labour's plans, which he said would have to be filled in by either tax, higher borrowing, or both:

-- The government's spending totals, which Labour has endorsed, include proceeds and savings from more privatisations, welfare reforms and pumping private finance into the National Health Service. Yet Clarke said Labour opposed these policies.

-- He said Labour had wrongly assumed that public spending would not be increased as a result of its promises to spend more on school repairs, to extend student loans and let local authorities spend money raised from the sale of public housing.
"Anyone who knows anything about government accounting knows that these Labour policies are indeed higher public spending and public borrowing," Clarke said.
-- He said Labour's plans to get 250,000 people off welfare and into work would cost more than the three billion pounds it has earmarked from a windfall tax on privatised utilities.
-- Brown is wrong to say abolishing tax relief on private medical insurance would completely finance its pledge to reduce value added tax on fuel to five percent from eight percent.
Brown's deputy, Alistair Darling, rejected Clarke's claims as "absolute nonsense" and said Labour would keep its promises.

"What we have put forward is a programme that adds up, one we know that we can deliver on. The difference between us and the Tory (Conservative) Party is that we will only make those promises we know we can deliver," he told Channel Four television. ($1=.6107 Pound)
